There is a heart in Aaron's chest that used to belong to someone else, and he lies awake at night listening to it as though it might tell him whose hands last held it. He pays a man in a car park for a name and a street, and is handed both, the way you're handed anything that costs money and shame in equal measure.

At the pool he learns her hours and makes his own match them until the coincidence wears thin and she stops pretending to notice. Within a fortnight he is in her house, and within a month he is telling her, badly, in her kitchen, what it is that beats under his ribs. She puts him out that night with everything he owns. Four days later she calls him back.

Somewhere else, before all of this or after it — it is hard to say which, the days run together for him now — a man walks up the steps of a police station and confesses to something at a crossing, to driving on a hundred yards and stopping and backing up and going anyway. He is returned to prison within the month. Later, released early on a recommendation nobody quite explains, he gets as far as the gate, sees his wife and the shape of his old life waiting for him, and keeps walking instead. He takes work far away, cleaning rooms at a motel where no one asks what he used to be.

He used to be certain of things. Ink on both forearms, boys on Saturdays learning to catch, a wife watching the weather in him build. Whether that came before the crossing or is only what's left after it isn't a thing the story troubles to date.

The woman at the pool, in her kitchen, has her own gap in her that nothing quite fills, though she doesn't say when it opened. A husband, two girls, a house with drawings taped to a wall — somewhere she had that, and somewhere she lost it, and now there is a bathroom door locked from the inside and a kitchen table where she does the same thing again with the girls' crayon suns still watching. She tells Aaron she cannot go on breathing in the same country as the man who did it, whoever he is, wherever he's got to. She says it until it is the only thing in the house.

He buys a pistol from a man in a lock-up. He drives to a motel he has been told about, out past the interstate, and finds a man behind it in the dark and gets him against the wall and cannot make his hand do what it came to do. The shot goes somewhere that will not kill. He tells the man to get up and run.

The man does not run far. He follows them back to their own room, bleeding through a shirt, and stands in the doorway asking to be finished, as if there were a debt outstanding and he is the only one still keeping the books. Aaron turns the gun round instead and puts it into his own chest, into the borrowed muscle, and it is only then, watching him go down, that anyone says the word crossing out loud, and Lena's mouth makes the shape of her husband's name, and the man on the floor makes the shape of an apology he has been carrying four hundred miles.

They get him into a car and drive with the horn down, and on the table the heart that came from somewhere else finally stops, having done its second borrowed stretch of time.

The man who confessed once, who fled once, who left once, goes back now to the family he walked out on, for good this time or only for now, no one says. The woman drives home alone, carrying something that has not happened yet and will take nine months to arrive, not knowing herself, some mornings, which of the men she buried first.

He wakes late with a headache and a strange flatness. There is nobody in his head who was not there two years ago. The clock says he has lost most of a day, and he can't account for the hole in it.

He was in a bookshop once, watching a woman with dyed hair laugh at a young man behind the counter. He remembers going in to make things up with her. That part is gone now, though he doesn't know it's gone.

He gets to the platform for work and gets on the other train instead. He cannot say why. He rides to the end of the line and walks out onto frozen sand, and a woman with dyed hair is already standing on it, as if she had been waiting, though neither of them would say that.

Two friends had handed him a form letter once, the clinic's letter, sent to everyone she knew. He does not remember the letter now. He does not remember going straight to the director's office and demanding the same thing be done to him that afternoon.

They drive back into the city talking too easily for strangers. Outside her building she asks him up for a drink as though it were the second time. It is, in a way neither of them can access.

He had filled two carrier bags once with everything that had her in it — a hairslide, a mug, a torn page — so a machine could find where the memories were pinned. He does not remember the bags. He does not remember handing them to Dr. Hallam.

In her flat they talk until it is late and she does not ask him to leave, and something in him that used to be careful is not careful now.

Two technicians let themselves into his old flat at night, once, and put the cap on him while he slept. One of them slid the bagged keepsakes into his own coat before the other noticed. That happened; it is simply no longer his.

Ivy touches his arm at the door and he does not flinch, though flinching used to be a thing he did without deciding to.

Inside his own head, once, he had stood in the worst of it — the shouting, the door, the dent in the car — and watched each room lose its walls while he was still in it, the ugly part going first.

They talk about nothing, an easy nothing, on her sofa.

Then the machine had reached the ones he wanted to keep, and he had run, carrying her out of her own memories and into places she had never been — a childhood kitchen, under a table, anywhere the map didn't go — because he had changed his mind and couldn't say so to anyone, least of all to himself.

She falls asleep on his shoulder; he doesn't wake her.

Outside, in the world that made this possible, two technicians had been drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear while the map on the screen stopped meaning anything, and neither of them noticed for a long time.

She invites him to stay, and he does.

The director had been called out at three in the morning to put it back on the rails, and the receptionist had kissed him in the hallway, and his wife, arriving behind him, told the receptionist exactly why she'd always felt that way about him and could not remember why.

Weeks pass, easy and unaccountable, the two of them behaving like people who already know each other, because they do, though they don't know that they do.

The last thing left, that night, was the shore house where they'd met — the window they broke, the boards they slept on. In the doorway of a room already dissolving, Ivy told him to walk out, and then to come and find her at the coast.

An envelope arrives one morning at Ivy's flat, and another at his old address, forwarded. Inside are transcripts, object lists, and a tape: the receptionist, quitting, emptying the filing cabinets on her way out, mailing every patient their own file.

They sit in the stairwell and play it. Their own voices telling two strangers exactly why they wanted each other erased — the drinking, the withholding, the dent in the car, the door. Ivy stands and walks halfway down the stairs and stops there a long time.

Then she comes back up.

They don't say anything about the beach, or the house, or what either of them paid to forget. They just go inside, and let the door close behind them, the way people do who have already decided, without needing to say so, to do it again.

The warehouse floor was cold under Danny's cheek, and the cold was the only thing that felt honest anymore.

Ash had his hand under Danny's head, saying nobody dies here today, and Danny believed him the way you believe things you need to be true. Blood was going out of him faster than the words were coming in, and he thought, absurdly, of a bathroom that never existed.

Pruitt had made him say it forty times. A bag of drugs, four dogs, a locked stall, until the lie stopped sounding rehearsed and started sounding like something that had actually happened to him once, in a life he could half remember. That was the whole trick of it, Pruitt said. You don't learn a story. You live in it until it's the only one you've got.

He'd told it in the bar with the laugh landing exactly where Pruitt promised it would, and Bram had looked at him the way a man looks at a tool he's deciding whether to buy, and that had been that. A name off a list. Elm. Not his choice, not anyone's — Bram dealt them out like cards, and Birch had argued for a full minute that his was the worst of the bunch, while the others laughed at him over eggs and coffee, arguing about whether a song about a girl was really about a girl and whether the waitress deserved anything extra for pouring it.

Ren had walked into that breakfast like a man walking into his own funeral reception, fresh off a stretch he could have shortened by talking and hadn't. Bram owed him for that silence, and the job was how he intended to pay it.

None of it mattered now except that the job had gone wrong in under a minute, alarms already screaming before the doors were open, Ash firing through glass in every direction while the car went down a street that led nowhere useful. Danny had run on foot until his legs quit being an option, dragged a woman from her car, and she'd had a gun in the door and put it in his stomach before he got the door shut. He'd shot her. He didn't like remembering that part. He was dying of it now, or near enough.

Birch had come in clean and furious, laying out the timings like a prosecutor, saying the police were on the pavement before any alarm could have tripped, which meant somebody in this room had made a call. Then he'd gone out into the dark and buried the stones somewhere only he could find them, trusting no one, not even the walls.

And then Ren, unbothered, opening his boot like he was unloading groceries, and out came a young cop named Doyle with his wrists tied and his eyes already understanding what kind of night this was. Ren had turned up an oldies station, danced two steps to it, taken the boy's ear with a razor blade and talked into the wound like it was a telephone, and then emptied a can of petrol over him for good measure.

Danny had done what he'd never planned to do. From the floor, gutshot, he'd emptied his gun into Ren before the match came down, and then he'd told Doyle, plainly, because the boy had earned that much — I'm police, there are cars outside waiting for Bram. Cal came back to a body and a story and decided the story held together well enough, then put three rounds into Doyle himself to make sure it never had to hold together for anyone else.

Bram arrived last, looked at Danny bleeding on the concrete, and said, flat as a verdict: that's him. Ash didn't hesitate. He put his gun on Bram instead, and Cal's came up, and all three fired at once, and when the noise stopped only Ash was still breathing beside Danny.

So now Danny told him. Everything. Ash listened to it with the whole of his face and then dragged himself up, gun to his own skull, firing it as the doors came down and the light poured in and cut him where he knelt.

MARCUS

Marcus and Rollo crossed the city arguing about what a hamburger was called abroad, and about foreign drug laws, and neither of them said a word about the job, because saying it made it real too early. In the corridor outside the flat they moved on to whether touching another man's wife's feet was worth being thrown off a balcony for, Marcus insisting there were lines even in this line of work. Then the door, the scripture Marcus recited to a boy named Tobin who had skimmed from Otis, the two shots, the briefcase lifted off the floor.

It was in the ringing quiet after that a man came out of the bathroom nobody had searched and emptied a revolver at them from six feet and hit nothing. Marcus stood in the spray of holes in the plaster behind him and called it divine intervention, and meant it, and from that morning on he was a different, quieter man.

He proved it that afternoon in a coffee shop, where two amateurs had just gotten up on the booth seats with a pistol out. Marcus let it be pointed at him. He handed over his own wallet, recited the passage again, told the pair what he had decided it meant, and let them walk. He kept the briefcase.

He carried it, still in borrowed shorts and a T-shirt because the car with Del's body in it had needed a man who timed things to the minute, into Otis's bar, where Otis was counting bills into an old boxer's hand and telling him which round to go down in.

ROLLO

Rollo was the one who bought the heroin, unusually pure, from a dealer named Kip, and shot it into his arm at the kitchen table before an evening out with Otis's wife. He took Nadia to a place where the waiters played at being someone else's decade, and the two of them won the dance contest with their shoes off. Back at his flat she found the bag in his coat and took it for something friendlier and went blue on the carpet, and it took a needle of adrenaline into her chest on Kip's floor to bring her back, while Rollo understood, too late, what he had nearly killed.

It was Rollo whose gun, in the car right after the Tobin job, went off over nothing at all and took the head off the man in the back seat. It was Marcus who drove them to Warren's after, where the fixer hosed them down in the yard and dressed them in borrowed clothes before the meeting with Otis.

And it was Rollo who was waiting in Denny's flat, sent to collect on a debt, with a submachine gun set down on the kitchen counter nearer to Denny than to himself.

DENNY

Long before any of it, a returning prisoner had sat a boy down and put his dead father's gold watch into his hands, and told him what it had cost to keep. Denny never afterward went anywhere without it.

He fought Otis's fixed fight and did not go down in the fifth. He won, and hit the man too hard, and was gone in a taxi before the crowd understood. In a motel room he asked Marielle whether she'd packed the watch and she had not, and so he went back for it, into a flat he should have known was watched, and it was there Rollo was waiting, and there Rollo died instead.

Driving off with the watch back on his wrist, Denny put the car through Otis at a crosswalk, and both wrecked, and both were dragged into a pawnshop basement by men who owned the shop. Denny broke free, was at the door, and turned back anyway, took a sword off the wall, and put a stop to what was happening to the man who had been hunting him. Otis told him after that they were square, provided he never came back.

He collected Marielle from the motel, put her on a motorcycle taken from the shop, and rode out of the city with the one thing, in the end, he had refused to leave behind.

The globe hit the boards and did not shatter so much as sigh, a small glassy exhalation, and Emmett Rusk was dead before it stopped rolling. The nurse found him an hour later with his mouth still shaped around the word he had said twice, once to the wife who wasn't there and once, at the end, to no one.

The newsreel ran that Friday in a screening room full of men who had never met him. Nine minutes: the mining money, the newspaper he'd bought on a whim, the governor's niece, the shopgirl, the opera house, the palace on the hill nobody had ever finished. It explained the shape of the fortune and none of the man, and the reporter Nash was told to go find out what "Bluebell" meant, since the family wouldn't say and the papers needed a last line.

He started with the second wife because she was easiest to find. Nora was in a nightclub by the sea at four in the afternoon, drunk in the particular unhurried way of someone with nowhere left to be drunk on the way to. She told him to get out before he'd finished his second sentence.

So Nash went backward instead. He read Barrow's memoir first, in a marble library that still smelled of new wood — the old banker's account of a woman at a kitchen table out west, signing her boy over the moment a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich, the father objecting from the doorway and being ignored, the boy driving a sled into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit him down before being taken east anyway. Barrow had written it almost fondly. *He never forgave me for the money,* the old man had put down, *and never once tried to give it back.*

He talked to Marsh, who remembered the twenty-fifth birthday, the reading of the estate, and Emmett choosing, out of everything, a newspaper that lost money because he thought it might be fun. He talked to Devlin, who described the bed moved into the office, the statement of principles set on the front page under Emmett's own signature, and then — much later, bitterer — the drunk half-sentence of a review he'd fallen asleep over, and how Emmett had finished it himself, printed it, and fired him inside the hour. "He kept every promise he ever wrote down," Devlin said, "which is the worst thing I can say about him."

Nash pieced together what the record didn't say. The staff hired away with money instead of merit, the party with the brass band. The marriage to Adele, the governor's niece, and the long silent breakfasts that followed it, each one a little further apart, until they were reading rival papers across a table that seemed to grow every week. The mud on Emmett's coat, the shopgirl laughing back at him, the secret rooms. Halloran climbing those stairs with Adele on his arm ten days before the election, offering silence for a resignation, and Emmett throwing him out instead — losing the governorship, the marriage, and Devlin's respect in the same bad month.

Then Nora, forced onto a stage she had no voice for, because he wanted the city to see him win something. Her debut, her poison, her one condition — never again — and Silvermount afterward, the ceilings too tall to heat, the crates never opened, she doing jigsaw puzzles alone on the floor of a hall built for a life that never arrived. The black-beach picnic nobody enjoyed. The morning she packed and he told her, in the only language he owned, that she could not go.

He talked to Nora once more, sober this time, and to the old butler Colm, who had found the boy — the man — with the wrecked bedroom and the glass globe, murmuring the word before he carried it past mirrors that gave him back smaller and smaller down the hall.

In the end Nash closed his notebook. No single word explains a life, he decided, and went to see the house cleared. Below him, workmen shoveled crates into a furnace, and among them, unremarked, a small sled with the name Bluebell painted along its side, the paint long gone to rust, went into the fire with everything else nobody had thought worth keeping.

The nurse found him an hour later with his mouth still shaped around the word he had said twice, once to the wife who wasn't there and once, at the end, to no one.

The newsreel ran that Friday in a screening room full of men who had never met him. Nine minutes: the mining money, the newspaper he'd bought on a whim, the governor's niece, the shopgirl, the opera house, the palace on the hill nobody had ever finished. It explained the shape of the fortune and none of the man, and the reporter Nash was told to go find out what "Bluebell" meant, since the family wouldn't say and the papers needed a last line.

He started with the second wife because she was easiest to find. Nora was in a nightclub by the sea at four in the afternoon, drunk in the particular unhurried way of someone with nowhere left to be drunk on the way to. She told him to get out before he'd finished his second sentence.

So Nash went backward instead. He read Barrow's memoir first, in a marble library that still smelled of new wood — the old banker's account of a woman at a kitchen table out west, signing her boy over the moment a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich, the father objecting from the doorway and being ignored, the boy driving a sled into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit him down before being taken east anyway. Barrow had written it almost fondly. *He never forgave me for the money,* the old man had put down, *and never once tried to give it back.*

He talked to Marsh, who remembered the twenty-fifth birthday, the reading of the estate, and Emmett choosing, out of everything, a newspaper that lost money because he thought it might be fun. He talked to Devlin, who described the bed moved into the office, the statement of principles set on the front page under Emmett's own signature, and then — much later, bitterer — the drunk half-sentence of a review he'd fallen asleep over, and how Emmett had finished it himself, printed it, and fired him inside the hour. "He kept every promise he ever wrote down," Devlin said, "which is the worst thing I can say about him."

Nash pieced together what the record didn't say. The staff hired away with money instead of merit, the party with the brass band. The marriage to Adele, the governor's niece, and the long silent breakfasts that followed it, each one a little further apart, until they were reading rival papers across a table that seemed to grow every week. The mud on Emmett's coat, the shopgirl laughing back at him, the secret rooms. Halloran climbing those stairs with Adele on his arm ten days before the election, offering silence for a resignation, and Emmett throwing him out instead — losing the governorship, the marriage, and Devlin's respect in the same bad month.

Then Nora, forced onto a stage she had no voice for, because he wanted the city to see him win something. Her debut, her poison, her one condition — never again — and Silvermount afterward, the ceilings too tall to heat, the crates never opened, she doing jigsaw puzzles alone on the floor of a hall built for a life that never arrived. The black-beach picnic nobody enjoyed. The morning she packed and he told her, in the only language he owned, that she could not go.

He talked to Nora once more, sober this time, and to the old butler Colm, who had found the boy — the man — with the wrecked bedroom and the glass globe, murmuring the word before he carried it past mirrors that gave him back smaller and smaller down the hall.

In the end Nash closed his notebook. No single word explains a life, he decided, and went to see the house cleared. Below him, workmen shoveled crates into a furnace, and among them, unremarked, a small sled with the name Bluebell painted along its side, the paint long gone to rust, went into the fire with everything else nobody had thought worth keeping.

Nadir stood at the counter with Sahar beside him, translating even the parts he understood, while the dealer behind the glass did an impression of his accent for the benefit of nobody. He bought the gun anyway. He left the shop armed and humiliated, and that should have been the end of it, except that a detective named Isaiah Reece would one day be called out to a roadside body and recognize the shoes on it before he recognized the face, and none of what happened after the gun shop would make sense without that morning still to come.

Two young men, Trey and Kwame, walked up a restaurant pavement talking about who was watching them and then took a prosecutor's car off him and his wife on the kerb outside. That night an officer named Boyle pulled over a couple named Hobart for nothing at all, had them out on the bonnet, and put his hand where it had no business going while the husband, Clay, stood three feet away and said nothing. His partner Voss watched the whole thing and went to their commander the next morning and said he couldn't ride with the man anymore. He was told he could have a new car if he said the problem was flatulence, and he took the deal, and believed, for a while, that this settled something.

A locksmith named Mateo fitted new locks at the prosecutor's house while the wife, Paula, stood at the top of the stairs telling her husband, loudly, that the tattooed one would be selling their keys to his friends by morning. Mateo went from there to Nadir's ruined-feeling shop and told him the lock was never the problem, that the door itself needed replacing, and Nadir heard a man inventing a second job for himself and threw him out. The door came off its hinges that same week. The insurer read the file and declined, on the grounds that he'd been warned.

Boyle sat across a desk from a clerk named Delia Frank, pleading for his father, and got a flat no, and lost his temper at her badge. Not long after, he would be the one crawling into an overturned, burning car to drag Renee Hobart out by her belt — the same hands. Neither of them would ever get to keep the simple version of the other.

Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham between parked vans, argued about it for two streets, and left him breathing outside a hospital. Weeks later, at a roadblock, four officers dragged Clay out of his own car at gunpoint, certain it was stolen, and Voss talked them down. Clay drove off afterward with Trey crouched in his passenger seat, drove too fast for either of their liking, and put him out on the verge without a word. What Trey did with that silence — buying Pham's van cheap, opening the back to find two dozen trafficked people instead of stock, driving them to the docks and turning them loose — none of it would happen for a little while yet, but it was already decided, somehow, in the way he stood on that dark verge afterward.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house with the pistol in his coat, and when Mateo came out he raised it, and Rosie ran off the porch into her father's arms as it went off. Nothing happened. Sahar, sent to buy ammunition, had quietly bought the box that does nothing. Nadir decided the child was his angel.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain, a hand moved toward a pocket, and Voss put two rounds into Kwame and burned the car. Reece found him by the roadside — his own brother — and his mother told him, on her kitchen floor, that she'd asked him a hundred times to go and look, and he never once did.

Paula fell down her own stairs with no one home, and told her housekeeper Alba, in the ambulance, that she was the only friend she had.

Snow came for the first time that winter. Two cars touched at a junction, and the shouting started before either driver looked at the damage.

I hadn't slept in six months when I found out that grief I had no right to would put me under. A church hall, folding chairs, a woman with a hand on my shoulder telling me it wasn't my fault, and me weeping about a disease I didn't have, and then eight hours of black, dreamless sleep. I went back four nights a week.

Then Ada started coming. Smoking through the meditation, faking it so badly I could see the lie in her, and once I could see it in her I could see it in myself, and the sleep stopped.

On a flight not long after, a soap salesman sat next to me and talked for forty minutes about how everything I owned had been chosen for me by people I'd never met. His name was Rex Marrow. I kept the card without meaning to.

I want to tell you now, out of order, about a window. Near the end. Ada is brought up to me by men with shaved heads who apologize and then leave us alone, and we stand holding hands while my face is wrapped in gauze, and outside the window the towers come down one after another, in sequence, like something rehearsed. I didn't know, that first night on the plane, that this was where the card in my pocket was going.

My flat went up while I was traveling — the windows on the pavement, the catalogue furniture gone with them. I called Rex instead of anyone else, and he took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing and no explanation. Outside a bar not long after, he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody in the car park and I had never felt anything so clearly.

It became a Tuesday thing, then a nightly thing, in a cellar under the bar, with rules read aloud before anybody threw a punch. Ada overdosed and rang the house; Rex went and brought her back, and then the two of them were loud through every floor of that building while I lay rigid below them, unable to say why it wounded me the way it did.

He was rendering fat from a cosmetic surgery clinic's dumpsters into soap on the kitchen stove and selling it back to the stores at eighty dollars a bar. He put lye on the back of my hand once and held it there and wouldn't let me go into the cave in my head the way I always did. Stay in the minute, he said. I have the mark still.

I blackmailed my employer with my own beaten face and got paid to disappear. The cellar became an organization with a name — Havoc — and the house filled with silent shaved men who broke into corporate buildings at night. I couldn't tell you when it stopped being mine.

Rex drove a car into oncoming traffic on a wet road, asking the men in back what they wished they'd done, and let it roll. When I came to in the ditch he was gone and stayed gone. Then Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill still in his hand, and I started trying to tear the whole thing down.

I went city to city and found the same cellar, the same rules on the same wall, and men who looked up and called me Rex Marrow to my face.

In a motel room with the flight records spread over the bed it went together: one body, one bank account, one man, awake and asleep. I called Ada and asked whose bed she'd been in. Mine, obviously, she said. Obviously.

I found the vans wired under the towers that held every debt record in the city. He walked me down a stairwell a flight at a time until I understood the gun in his hand was in mine, and I put it in my mouth and fired through my cheek to be rid of him.

Then Ada, the window, the buildings going down in order, exactly as I'd already told you.

All night the helicopters went over the city, low and patient, dusting the fruit fly out of every yard, and everybody in every house heard the same drone at the same hour and did not think of it again.

Neil Hartigan changed his shirt twice while his wife Bess finished a canvas full of unfinished bodies, both of them dreading the guest list a little.

Otto the baker wrote a name and an age on a card — Charlie Rill, seven — and told the mother it would be ready Monday, please collect it promptly.

On his way to school Charlie stepped off the kerb and a waitress named Rhona, late for her shift, caught him with the wing of her car. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift, and walked the rest of the way home.

That evening he lay down on the sofa and did not wake properly. After that there was a room with a machine in it, and Grant and Elaine took shifts in the chair beside it.

Into that corridor came Duff, the father Grant hadn't seen in years, with a paper coffee cup and nothing to say, so he told his son about a woman from decades back, an affair, as if it might help.

No one came for the cake and no one paid for it, and Otto, unpaid and unable to bear being ignored, began telephoning the house at two in the morning to say the boy's name into the receiver.

Across town Cheryl folded laundry with the phone against her ear, murmuring men through their fantasies, while her husband Stu sat three feet away going quietly incandescent.

Stu and three friends, Vern among them, walked in to the good water and found a young woman face down in the shallows. They tied a line round her ankle so she wouldn't drift, and fished for two more days before telling anyone.

When Vern told it the way it got told at the pub, his wife Iris, wiping clown paint from her face at the kitchen table, stopped with the sponge in her hand, disgusted.

Nightly the singer Vida performed under low lights to people who mostly talked through her, while at home her daughter Bee practiced cello alone in an empty house.

Officer Rowe, needing an alibi for his hours with Nan, drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and put it out, then told Peg it must have jumped the fence.

Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, found out about the new man and spent an afternoon sawing every chair and table she owned into pieces.

House-sitting the Hartigans' good address, Ike and Dot made each other up as corpses and photographed themselves lying dead in the hall, laughing.

At the dinner party, over the fish, Bess told Neil about the modelling session and then the affair after it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made a scene in front of everyone.

In the morning they switched off Charlie's machine. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to shout at Otto about the calls, and he sat them down, put warm bread in front of them, and grieved with strangers who had lost what he hadn't known was theirs.

Bee came home from rehearsal, found her mother asleep in the chair as always, and walked out to the garage, pulled the door down, and left the engine running.

At a picnic in the hills, a girl said some ordinary wrong thing, and Stu, who had been holding something since the river, picked up a rock and brought it down on her.

That evening the ground moved for eleven seconds, and by the late bulletin it had gathered everything into itself — the boy, the dog, the furniture, the girl in the river and the one in the hills, the dinner party and the garage and the corridor confession — folded into three minutes of news, indistinguishable from weather, as if the whole city had simply been shaken once, gently, and told to go back to sleep.

Above the noise, at an open window, the old man was still talking. He had been talking for a while, in the patient, unhurried way of someone who has stopped expecting to be believed. Nothing survives, he said. Not the body, not the memory of the body, not the memory of the memory. It isn't a complaint. It's just how the hours are built. The younger man beside him said nothing and looked down at the blue light filling the street below.

That light was for two men being carried out through a crowd with their hands cuffed behind them, one shouting, one silent. The crowd parted for them the way crowds do, already forgetting their faces.

An hour before, the man now silent had been swinging a fire extinguisher long after there was any reason to. He hadn't stopped when the man beneath him stopped moving. A few feet off, watching with the same idle interest as everyone else, stood the man they had actually come to find — not the one Jonah had killed, but the one whose arm Cort had broken first, in the dark of the club, mistaking a stranger's face for a stranger's face.

They'd gone into that basement on the word of two men who'd stepped out of a doorway and asked for money in exchange for a name and an address. Cort had paid without hesitating. He had been in that mood for a while — since the ambulance, since the trolley and the blanket and the face on it that both he and Jonah had recognized coming out of the party laughing.

Before that, there had been the party itself: Cort drinking past the point of usefulness, working the room while Lise watched him do it and then simply left, collecting her coat without a word, because she had seen this before and knew there was no arguing with it that night. She had not planned to walk home alone. She had planned, an hour earlier, to be arguing cheerfully with both men on the underground about sex and about how much Cort had already had to drink — an argument built for people who expect to have it again tomorrow.

She hadn't wanted to cross four lanes of headlights, so she'd taken the underpass instead. Halfway along the tiled tunnel a man had a woman by the hair and was explaining something to her with his fist. He turned when he heard her. He didn't hurry. When it was over he went on hitting her head against the concrete, and a man at the far end of the tunnel looked, hesitated, and walked away.

Before any of that, there had been an afternoon in the park: sprinklers turning over the grass, children running through the spray, Lise on her side with a book she wasn't really reading, one hand flat on her stomach, the day entirely unspoiled.

She had found out that morning. Alone in the flat, sitting on the edge of the bath with the stick in both hands, she had let herself smile at it before telling anyone at all.

And before that, in bed, with thin light through the curtains, she had told Cort about the dream — the tunnel, red-lit, that she kept walking into and couldn't get out of — and they had teased each other lazily about Jonah, who used to share the flat and her bed and was now only a friend who slept on the sofa when he stayed too late. Three of them, easy with one another, no idea yet what the day held.

The old man at the window said it again, as if repeating it might make the boy beside him understand it sooner than he himself had. Nothing survives. Not the tunnel, not the sprinklers, not the small flat weight of a hand against a stomach.

Below them the street was clearing. The blue light pulled away. In a little while there would be nothing to mark where any of it had happened — no blood on the tiles that couldn't be hosed off, no bruise that wouldn't yellow and fade, no name that would matter to anyone by morning except the ones who had to carry it.

I. TIGRE

Four adults, a baby, and a dog in a house built for two. Ruben slept on the couch and watched his brother's wife move through the kitchen and told himself it was only watching. Nestor came home from the chemist's with a scarf smell still on him and knocked Alma across the room for asking about money, and Ruben started saying, quietly at first, that she should come away with him.

The dog changed things. Tigre came back off the street having killed something bigger than itself, and a neighbour told Ruben what that was worth. Within a month the dog was going into a pit twice a week and coming out every time, and Ruben was hiding money in the wardrobe like a man building a door.

He paid two men in a bar to open that door for him. Nestor came out of hospital, worked out who'd sent them in about a day, and left with his wife, his son, and every note Ruben had saved.

The dog outlasted the plan. In a last fight the promoter Chaco, having lost too much on one bout, put a pistol into Tigre's side in the ring. Ruben went over the rope with a knife and was in the truck with Pipo before the crowd moved, the dog bleeding across the back seat, and at sixty through a red light the truck took the side out of a small car turning across the junction.

A vagrant named Cardo, pushing a scrap cart through the smoke, looked at the wrecks and the running people and lifted the bleeding dog out of the back seat and carried it away.

He nursed it in a yard full of strays, feeding it by hand for weeks, until it slept against him and followed him into the street each morning — the only thing he had ever kept alive on purpose.

Then one evening he came home to a yard of dead dogs and Tigre standing among them with its muzzle wet. He held the gun to its head a long time and could not fire it, and sat down on the ground instead.

Shaved, in clothes that didn't fit him, he later walked out into the flat grey wasteland at the city's edge with the dog beside him and nowhere in particular to go.

II. CELINE

Hector left his wife and daughters at a birthday party and moved Celine into a flat with a floor-to-ceiling window facing her own billboard, so that she woke each morning to her own face across the street.

She was in a small car at a junction when a truck ran the light. She woke in hospital with a cage of steel pins in her leg and asked first about Chispa, her lapdog, lost somewhere in the unfamiliar flat.

The dog had gone through a gap in the boards and could not get back, its whining rising through every room. Hector tore the floor up plank by plank while her leg went untreated and turned bad above him.

It came off above the knee. The same week the billboard across the road was stripped and pasted over, and the two of them sat in the wrecked flat looking at the blank frame where she used to be.

III. RUBEN AND ALMA

Nestor went into a bank with the same scarf and was shot on the floor of it. At the funeral Ruben made his offer one last time, and Alma looked at him and said no and meant it, and he understood then that she never would have come.

IV. CARDO AND HIS OWN

Elian met him behind a church and handed him a photograph of his own half-brother Sergio, naming a price and asking no questions. Cardo took the man off a pavement without difficulty, then drove him not to a grave but to his yard, chaining him among the empty kennels instead of finishing the job.

Before that, he had stood far back at his wife's burial among people who believed him twenty years dead, then followed his grown daughter Perla three streets home and stopped outside her door, saying nothing.

He went back for Elian, sat the brothers down across from each other, put a loaded pistol on the floor exactly between them, and walked out having taken money from both.

Then he let himself into Perla's flat while she was out, sat an hour on her bed, and left on her machine a long confession of who he was, what he'd done, and why — and took one photograph from the shelf on his way out.

He left the money on her table. The dog was waiting at the door. Together they walked out into the grey ground at the edge of the city, and did not look back toward anything they had left standing.

Solly Two Coats walked into the diamond house dressed as a pilgrim, head bowed with three men who prayed like they meant it, and walked out with the finest stone any of them had ever touched. By the time they'd shed the robes in an alley, Marv was already on the phone from overseas, telling him to bring it straight over, no delays, no cleverness.

Solly flew in and went first to Hersch, who took the stone into his workshop with the calm of a man used to holding other people's crimes. Only then did Solly head to the bookmaker's, an empty case swinging from his hand, to lay a bet on a fight he didn't know was already rotten.

That fight had been arranged weeks earlier, in its own way. Grigor the Nail had sent Solly toward the bookmaker's and, in the same breath, told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno there was easy money to be had there. Neither side knew they were walking toward each other. Around the same time, Halloway and Digby sent Pretty Sam to buy a caravan from the travellers' camp, and Sam, contemptuous as always, picked a fight with a quiet man named Finn and was knocked cold for his trouble. That left Halloway with no fighter for Coldstone's fixed bout, and no choice but to put Finn in himself, promising Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth.

At the bookmaker's, Ike, Benno and Tulley bungled everything, grabbing Solly's arm and his case in a panic and fleeing straight into Grigor, who'd come to see how his little trap had played out. Solly went with Grigor. The case did not have the stone in it — Solly had already left that with Hersch — and Grigor, refusing to believe it, took the arm off to force the lock. He found nothing. He'd mutilated a man over an empty box.

Across the fight venue, Finn ignored every instruction and put his man down in the first round, costing Coldstone a fortune. Coldstone took it out on Halloway, and then, hearing what Grigor had done and hadn't found, fed Solly to his pigs, warning Halloway and Digby what would happen if the second fight went wrong too.

By then Marv had flown in, found no cousin and no stone, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge, a man who tracked fools rather than professionals. Ledge found Ike and Benno easily enough, shot their car apart, and took them and the stone they'd somehow retrieved along the way.

Halloway and Digby, desperate, told Finn again to go down in the fourth. Coldstone's men, unsatisfied with threats alone, burned Finn's mother to death in her caravan, turning coercion into blood debt.

Grigor, still hunting the stone he'd already destroyed a man for, ambushed Ledge's car. In the gunfire that followed, Ledge, Grigor and Benno all died. Only Tulley walked away, and with him went the dog — the same one that had, in all the chaos back at the bookmaker's, swallowed the diamond whole without anyone noticing.

The second fight came. Finn waited, this time, until the fourth round exactly — then knocked his man out anyway, while the travellers, armed and grieving, cut down Coldstone's men through the crowd. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone afterward and shot him. By morning the travellers had vanished, taking their dead and their debts with them.

Tulley's dog, however, turned up days later at a pet shop, handed in by someone who didn't want it. The shopkeeper found it had swallowed something hard and shining, and coughed the truth up onto the counter. Halloway and Digby, who had never once gone near the diamond house in the north, ended up holding the very stone that had started it all.

Listen: he has come unstuck in time, and there is no reliable way to say what happened before what, because for him nothing did.

He is on the lecture platform, telling a crowd about the fourth dimension, about how every moment always exists and always will, when the beam weapon finds him and he dies exactly as he always knew he would. This is not the end. It is simply one of the places he is.

He is a boy in a small industrial town, weak and peculiar, and his father is throwing him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim. He sinks. At the bottom he discovers he does not mind staying there.

He is in a transparent enclosure on another planet with a film actress, and the aliens who keep them are explaining, patiently, the way one explains something to a child who keeps forgetting, that free will is a notion peculiar to his own small planet, that every instant exists all at once and always will, and that his death — which he has seen — is only a bad moment among the good ones, no more permanent than any other.

He is a conscripted chaplain's assistant, shipped overseas with no training worth the name, and then he is lost behind the lines with a scout who beats him for asking to be left to die. Later — or earlier — the scout is dying of gangrene on a train full of prisoners, and with his last breath he blames the boy for everything.

He is being held in a camp beside enemy officers who have drawn double rations for years through an error no one has bothered to correct, their health an absurdity beside the exhaustion of the new arrivals.

He is in a disused abattoir in a great city, sleeping in the meat locker with the other prisoners, and then the city is gone, burned to nothing in a single night, and they climb up into a world made of ash.

He is digging bodies out of cellars with the others until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves, right there in the rubble, and no one is surprised.

He is collapsed in a hospital bed at home, and another patient hands him novels by a hack science fiction writer, paperbacks with lurid covers, and something in them fits the shape of what he cannot otherwise say.

Somewhere in the prison system, before or after all this, a man who has taken up the dead scout's grievance as his own promises, almost gently, that he will have him killed one day, whenever the day comes. The man is patient. He has time. Everyone, it turns out, has time.

He is marrying the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school, and he becomes rich, and this seems to happen to someone else, a man wearing his name.

He is surviving a plane crash in the mountains while his wife, driving frantically to reach the hospital, dies of exhaust fumes in her own car. He is fine. He is always, infuriatingly, fine.

He is on a radio talk show, trying to explain the aliens, the zoo, the actress, the fourth dimension, to a host who does not know what to do with his voice.

His daughter is deciding he is senile, taking his checkbook and his keys, believing this is mercy.

None of this comes with dates. No one ages visibly across the telling; no cause visibly produces its effect, though later he will say the scout's blame produced the promise, and the promise produced the beam weapon, and the crash produced nothing at all, being only another moment sitting where it always sat. He does not experience these things in a row. He experiences them the way a man experiences a card he has just been dealt from a deck already printed, face up, in an order no one shuffled and no one can now unshuffle.

So it goes. He is born in the industrial town. He is dying on the platform. He is in the zoo. He is at the bottom of the pool, not minding it at all.

Emlyn came to Wilder's house the same evening, and told him, without any particular emphasis, that he had known for four years. He had known since the trip abroad, when Odile told him everything in a hotel room while the shutters banged in a wind off the sea. He said he had never thought much of Wilder's letters either — the ones held for her at the desk, the ones written in a hand the concierge and then the husband had both recognized at a glance.

Wilder had summoned him in a state, an hour before, ringing from a telephone in the hall as though the wire itself might buckle under what he had to say. He had not expected this answer. He had expected to be the one confessing.

It was Odile who had put him into that state. In a bar two years after the rooms had closed, she had told him, quite calmly, over a glass she did not finish, that her marriage was over, and that the previous night she had told her husband everything — as if for the first time. She had let slip, almost as an afterthought, that Emlyn had for some time been publishing a writer Wilder represented, a man they both privately despised, and the two of them had apparently gone on doing business, lunching, corresponding, all the while.

That detail was what undid Wilder. Not the end of the marriage — he had expected that eventually — but the sense that a whole second history had been running alongside the one he knew, men speaking to each other in rooms he wasn't in.

Before that bar, before the end, there had been two years of the rented rooms: the plates they'd chosen together, the linen, the ordinary Tuesdays. Odile had announced, in that flat, cheerful voice she used for consequential things, that she was carrying her husband's child, and they had decided, without much discussion, that the rooms would go on exactly as before. And they had — until the rooms themselves became a kind of chore, an obligation neither of them wanted to keep dressing as romance, and they split the crockery between them and gave up the lease without any confession forcing their hand.

Long before that, of course, there had been the party at Emlyn's own house, where Wilder had led her upstairs while the others drank below and told her, with the particular gentleness of a man crossing a line he has already decided to cross, how lovely she was.

And before Wilder ever knew what Emlyn knew, there had been the long lunch — the two men drinking through a whole afternoon at a restaurant, Emlyn baiting his friend about contemporary fiction, cruel and funny and entirely unrevealing, while the thing he knew sat between them like a third guest neither would name. He had known since the trip abroad, when Odile told him everything in a hotel room while the shutters banged in a wind off the sea. He said he had never thought much of Wilder's letters either — the ones held for her at the desk, the ones written in a hand the concierge and then the husband had both recognized at a glance.

She had let slip, almost as an afterthought, that Emlyn had for some time been publishing a writer Wilder represented, a man they both privately despised, and the two of them had apparently gone on doing business, lunching, corresponding, all the while.
